transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?

Hello, doctor. I'm here because during long meetings or when I’m working through complex plans, my mind keeps drifting off and I miss important details even though I’m really trying to pay attention. It has started to get in the way of my work, so I wanted to get some professional insight on why my focus is slipping.
Do you find yourself fidgeting, feeling restless, or having difficulty waiting your turn in situations, or is it mainly the difficulty with sustaining focus on tasks that's troubling you?

It is definitely the difficulty with sustaining focus and my mind drifting off, rather than physical restlessness or fidgeting. While I don't feel physically restless, I do sometimes catch myself talking over people or dominating conversations when I get excited about a project. Ultimately, it's the struggle to stay focused on dense work and long meetings that is truly impacting my life.

Can you tell me more about what happens when you catch yourself talking over people or dominating conversations - is this something that you've always done, or is it a relatively new behavior for you?

I think I’ve always had a tendency to get overly enthusiastic, but it has become much more noticeable and problematic over the last two years as my professional and community roles expanded. In smaller meetings, I’ll get excited about a project and give way more detail than anyone asked for, only realizing I'm dominating the conversation when I notice people looking at the clock.

Can you think of any situations where you've acted on impulse without fully considering the consequences, such as blurting out answers or interrupting others, aside from talking over people in conversations?

Honestly, I can't really think of any other situations where I act impulsively or without thinking. Aside from that tendency to talk over people and dominate conversations when I get excited about a project, I don't really have those kinds of impulsive behaviors.
Can you describe how your difficulties with focus and your tendency to dominate conversations have changed or developed over time, especially in relation to any significant life events or stressors?

These focus issues actually go back to childhood—my elementary school report cards always mentioned daydreaming and losing homework—but they’ve become much more problematic over the last two years as my workload and community projects expanded. My usual spreadsheets and coping systems are getting overwhelmed by these high-stakes responsibilities, making my old habits of drifting off and over-talking much more visible. It's just become much harder to manage everything now that the stakes are higher.
Do you still find joy or interest in activities that you used to enjoy, or has your enthusiasm and pleasure in these activities decreased over time?

I still have plenty of interest and enthusiasm for my work and my community activities, and I care about them deeply. My main struggle is definitely just staying focused and keeping up with everything, rather than any loss of pleasure in doing them.
Can you estimate how often your difficulties with focus and conversations occur, and how significantly they interfere with your daily life and relationships, on a scale from mild to severe?

These focus and conversation issues happen almost daily, especially during long meetings, and have been a noticeable problem for nearly two years. While I’d rate the overall severity as mild, it has a significant impact on my confidence; coworkers have started quietly double-checking my work, and I've even turned down new leadership roles. Catching myself dominating conversations in smaller groups only adds to that worry.

Can you describe any significant symptoms of hyperactivity, such as fidgeting or feeling constantly 'on the go', that you may have exhibited as a child, which could help differentiate between possible conditions?

I don't recall having hyperactive symptoms like fidgeting or feeling "on the go" when I was a child. Instead, my struggles back then were more about daydreaming, losing worksheets, and being forgetful, which my teachers often noted on my report cards. My parents even used to joke that I’d forget my head if it wasn't attached to my shoulders.

Do you experience any symptoms of hyperactivity now, such as feeling restless, having trouble engaging in quiet leisure activities, or being constantly on the go, that might not have been present in your childhood?

No, I don't really experience physical restlessness, trouble keeping still, or feeling like I'm constantly driven by a motor. My challenges nowadays are much more related to my focus and attention, along with occasionally talking too much when I get excited about a project.

You've mentioned that you don't experience significant physical restlessness or hyperactivity now, but can you think of any situations, perhaps under stress or in certain environments, where you might exhibit more hyperactive behaviors, such as excessive talking, even beyond the context of being excited about a project?

I really only struggle with excessive talking in smaller meetings or community group settings when we are actively discussing projects. In those moments, I'll catch myself talking over others and giving way too much detail until I notice people checking the clock. Outside of those project-focused discussions, I don't experience any other hyperactive or physically restless behaviors.
Can you recall any instances where you had to repeat instructions or re-read material because you didn't catch the details the first time, and if so, how often does this happen to you?

Yes, this happens very frequently. During long meetings, my mind drifts after 10 to 15 minutes, and I'll completely miss key deadlines or decisions that were just discussed. Also, when reviewing reports or emails, I tend to skim rather than deeply read, which leads to me missing details like a wrong date or a miscalculated spreadsheet column that my team then has to correct.
Can you describe any specific strategies or techniques you use to help you stay focused during long meetings or when working on complex tasks, and how effective you find them to be?

I rely heavily on detailed checklists, color-coded spreadsheets, and keeping my phone filled with reminder notes, which used to work well before my workload expanded. Now, these strategies aren't enough; I still make errors on my spreadsheets despite the color-coding, find half-written reminders on my phone but still miss tasks, and my mind still drifts off 10 to 15 minutes into long meetings.

Can you think of any situations where you've had difficulty with organization, time management, or self-regulation of emotions, beyond just the focus issues and dominating conversations you've mentioned, that might be impacting your daily life?

I don't struggle with emotional self-regulation, but organization and planning are definitely major battles for me. When managing clinic rollouts and community projects, I often get paralyzed trying to prioritize, bouncing aimlessly between emails and calendars without finishing anything in order. I also tend to procrastinate on dense tasks by doing quick chores, and despite my phone reminders, I still occasionally forget to return calls, pay bills, or show up to meetings.

Can you tell me more about how your difficulties with focus and organization impact your daily routines and tasks outside of work and community projects, such as managing personal chores, finances, or maintaining your living space?

These difficulties definitely spill over into my personal life, as my phone is constantly filled with half-written reminder notes because I will completely forget to return a call or pay a bill if I don't write it down immediately. Even with all these reminders, I still occasionally miss things and only realize it when someone follows up with me.

Can you clarify if your difficulties with focus, such as daydreaming and missing details, are primarily due to distractibility or an inability to sustain attention on tasks, and do you notice any difference in these symptoms when you're working on tasks that are highly interesting versus those that are less engaging?

It is really a combination of both; my mind easily drifts to other thoughts or tasks during meetings, but I also find it exhausting to sit down and sustain focus on dense, complex documents. While I struggle significantly more with dry, unengaging tasks like reading thick policy documents, my focus can still slip even during projects and discussions that I care about deeply.

Have you experienced any symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity in multiple settings, such as at work, at home, or in social situations, and if so, can you describe how these symptoms have impacted your daily life across these different contexts?

Yes, these issues definitely show up across all areas of my life. At work, my spreadsheet errors and drifting in meetings have led to coworkers double-checking my work, which has eroded my confidence to the point of turning down new leadership opportunities. In my personal and community life, I get overwhelmed juggling projects, talk too much in groups, and frequently forget to pay bills, return calls, or attend board meetings unless I write them down immediately.

Can you think of any situations where you exhibited impulsive behaviors, such as interrupting others, blurting out answers, or acting without much consideration for consequences, aside from talking over people in conversations, that might have occurred at any point in your life?

Besides my tendency to talk over people or get overly carried away when talking about projects, I don't really recall acting impulsively. I've never been one to blurt things out or act without considering the consequences of my actions. It really has just been that issue with dominating conversations when I get excited.

Can you recall any instances where you felt an overwhelming urge to do something impulsively, such as spending money recklessly, acting on impulse without considering consequences, or engaging in risky behaviors, at any point in your life?

No, I don't recall ever having those kinds of impulsive urges, reckless spending habits, or engaging in risky behaviors. I've always been quite careful in those areas, so that kind of impulsivity hasn't been an issue for me at all.

Can you think of any situations where you felt like you were able to focus and sustain attention without much effort, and if so, what made those situations different from the ones where you struggle with focus?

Honestly, I find it hard to think of any situations where focusing comes effortlessly to me. Even when I am deeply interested in the work, I still have to rely heavily on tools like detailed spreadsheets and checklists to keep myself on track. It always feels like staying focused requires a great deal of conscious effort, no matter the task.

Can you elaborate on how your symptoms of inattention and impulsivity, such as difficulty sustaining focus and talking over people, impact your relationships and daily functioning, and do you feel like these symptoms are causing significant distress or impairment in your life?

In smaller meetings or community groups, I often dominate conversations and talk over people, only realizing it when I notice others checking the clock. This, along with my missed details, has led to coworkers quietly double-checking my work and taking over pieces of projects, which has deeply eroded my confidence. It causes me real distress, and I've even started turning down new leadership opportunities because I worry I can no longer reliably keep everything straight.

Can you help me understand how you think your symptoms, particularly the difficulty with focus and the tendency to dominate conversations, would be classified as 'mild' given the significant impact they have on your work, relationships, and personal confidence?

I think they might be classified as "mild" because I've managed to compensate well enough with my spreadsheets and checklists to keep my job and avoid any major professional or personal crises. I am still functioning as a manager, but the constant, conscious effort just to stay afloat is exhausting and has forced me to pull back from new opportunities.

Can you clarify what specific aspects of your symptoms or their impact on your life lead you to describe them as 'mild', despite the significant effects on your work, relationships, and personal confidence?

I consider it "mild" because I haven't faced any catastrophic crises—I haven't been fired, my marriage is fine, and I've built a successful career using coping tools like spreadsheets and checklists. However, it still feels heavy because those systems are reaching their limit, eroding my confidence as colleagues have to quietly double-check my work. It has reached a point where I'm turning down new leadership opportunities because I'm worried I can't reliably keep everything straight anymore.

Can you help me understand what specific criteria you're using to judge the severity of your symptoms as 'mild', given the significant impact they have on your daily functioning and personal confidence?

I consider it "mild" because I haven't faced a major crisis, lost my job, or had a complete breakdown, thanks to years of compensating with spreadsheets and checklists. However, even without a single catastrophe, the accumulation of these small lapses is seriously eroding my confidence and forcing me to turn down new leadership roles. That is why, even if it seems mild on paper, it feels very significant to me now.

Can you elaborate on what specific factors or events might trigger your symptoms to worsen or improve, as understanding these patterns could help clarify the nature of your difficulties with focus and conversation?

My focus issues definitely worsen during long strategy meetings, when I'm juggling too many projects, or during mentally exhausting tasks like writing proposals. In conversations, my tendency to over-talk is triggered in smaller meetings when I'm highly passionate about the project. I try to improve things by using spreadsheets, checklists, and phone reminders, but those coping systems are currently overwhelmed by my heavy workload.

Can you think of any instances where you exhibited a combination of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, such as feeling restless and having trouble sustaining focus, that might help differentiate between possible conditions?

While I don't really feel physically restless, I do experience a combination of losing focus and talking excessively. In meetings, my mind will drift off and I'll completely lose track of the discussion. Then, once I do start talking about a project, I'll find myself interrupting others, over-explaining, and dominating the conversation before I even realize it.

Can you think of any situations where you have exhibited both significant inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms simultaneously, such as feeling restless while also having difficulty sustaining focus, which could help clarify whether your primary issue is more with attention or impulsivity?

I don't really experience physical restlessness or hyperactivity in that way, so I can't think of a situation where both of those occurred together. My main struggle is definitely with my mind drifting and losing focus, though I do sometimes catch myself talking too much in meetings.

Can you help me understand how you differentiate between the impact of your focus issues and your tendency to dominate conversations on your daily life and relationships, as both seem to significantly affect your confidence and interactions?

My focus issues primarily impact my professional reliability and self-confidence, as having colleagues double-check my work has made me decline new leadership roles out of fear of making mistakes. In contrast, dominating conversations affects me more socially and interpersonally, leaving me feeling self-conscious when I realize I'm talking over others and people are checking the clock. While one makes me worry about my competence, the other makes me feel like I'm dominating the space instead of truly collaborating.

Can you think of any situations where you exhibited clear signs of hyperactivity, such as fidgeting, feeling restless, or an inability to engage in activities quietly, that were not related to excitement about a project or conversation?

No, I really don't experience physical restlessness, fidgeting, or an inability to be quiet. My challenges are almost entirely related to my mind drifting, losing focus, and managing details rather than any kind of physical hyperactivity.

Can you recall any childhood behaviors or symptoms that might suggest you had more hyperactive or impulsive tendencies, even if they are not present now, to help differentiate between possible conditions?

No, I don't recall having any hyperactive or impulsive behaviors as a child. My struggles back then were strictly related to inattention, like daydreaming in class, losing worksheets, and forgetting to turn in my homework. In fact, I was so forgetful that my parents always joked I would forget my head if it wasn't attached to my shoulders.

Can you think of any situations, past or present, where you might have exhibited symptoms of both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity simultaneously, which could help clarify the nature of your difficulties?

In meeting settings, I definitely experience a mix of both. On one hand, my mind easily drifts off and I miss key details, but on the other hand, especially in smaller group discussions, I tend to get overly excited, talk excessively, and interrupt or dominate the conversation without realizing it.
